questions.text: During an engine failure on a cross-country, a pilot needs to land immediately. The only suitable field is across an active Class D airport boundary — entering the airspace without radio contact is normally prohibited. Under 14 CFR 91.3(b), what authority does the PIC have in this situation?

options.label: A
options.text: The PIC must attempt radio contact on the Class D frequency before entering — if no contact is established within 30 seconds, the pilot may enter the airspace and land, but must file an incident report within 48 hours

options.label: B
options.text: The PIC may deviate from ANY regulation to the extent required to meet the emergency — this includes entering Class D without communication, landing without clearance, and using any runway regardless of active winds

options.label: C
options.text: The PIC cannot enter Class D airspace without a clearance, even in an emergency — the correct procedure is to land in the field short of the Class D boundary, even if it is less suitable than the airport runway

options.label: D
options.text: The PIC may enter the Class D airspace, but only if they squawk 7700 first — without the emergency transponder code, ATC has no way to know the aircraft is in distress and cannot protect the airspace

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.3(b) states: 'In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the pilot in command may deviate from any rule of this part to the extent required to meet that emergency.' This authority is absolute and self-executing — it does not require prior permission, radio contact, or transponder codes. The PIC's emergency authority covers airspace violations, unauthorized landings, runway selection, and any other deviation necessary for safety. The FAA may request a written report after the fact, but survival and safe landing are the priorities during the emergency. Squawking 7700 is recommended procedure but NOT a prerequisite for exercising emergency authority. The 'try radio contact first' answer fabricates a 30-second waiting requirement. The 'no entry without clearance' answer incorrectly limits PIC emergency authority. The 'squawk first' answer incorrectly makes squawk 7700 a legal prerequisite.

questions.text: A Cessna 172 POH lists the best glide speed (Vg) as 65 knots at maximum gross weight of 2,550 lbs. The aircraft is currently at 2,100 lbs with two occupants and partial fuel. After an engine failure, what is the most accurate best glide speed for this lighter weight?

options.label: A
options.text: The Vg cannot be determined in flight — only the published max-gross-weight figure is valid, and attempting to fly a modified Vg introduces unacceptable error into the glide calculation

options.label: B
options.text: 65 knots — Vg is a fixed airspeed that does not change with weight because the wing's L/D ratio is determined by the airfoil shape, not the aircraft's mass

options.label: C
options.text: Approximately 73 knots — at lighter weights, the aircraft must fly faster to generate the same L/D ratio because the wing is producing less lift per unit of dynamic pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Approximately 59 knots — Vg decreases as weight decreases because less lift is needed, which reduces induced drag, shifting the L/D max point to a lower airspeed

questions.explanation: The published best glide speed (Vg) is calculated at maximum gross weight. At lighter weights, the aircraft requires less lift to sustain flight, which means less induced drag at any given airspeed. Since L/D max (the point of minimum total drag) shifts to a lower airspeed when induced drag is reduced, Vg decreases. The rule of thumb is approximately 1% Vg decrease per 2% weight decrease below max gross. At 2,100 lbs (82% of 2,550 max gross), that's an 18% weight reduction → approximately 9% Vg reduction → 65 × 0.91 ≈ 59 knots. The '65-knot fixed' answer incorrectly states L/D ratio is independent of weight — the L/D ratio is a function of AOA, and the AOA for maximum L/D corresponds to a lower speed at lighter weights. FAA-H-8083-25C Chapter 5 describes the weight-Vg relationship.

questions.text: After an engine failure at 3,000 feet AGL, a pilot trims for best glide and identifies a suitable field 2 miles away. The pilot is slightly low on the glide path and pulls back on the yoke to 'stretch the glide' and reach the field. Beyond the misconception, what specific aerodynamic consequence makes this the wrong action?

options.label: A
options.text: Pulling back has no aerodynamic effect because the propeller is windmilling, creating a constant drag force that dominates the glide performance regardless of the aircraft's pitch attitude

options.label: B
options.text: Pulling back momentarily increases lift, which causes the aircraft to balloon upward and then sink rapidly when the excess lift dissipates, creating an oscillating phugoid that makes field selection impossible

options.label: C
options.text: Pulling back increases the angle of attack, which spikes induced drag exponentially — total drag increases, the glide ratio WORSENS, the descent angle STEEPENS, and the aircraft lands SHORTER than if Vg had been maintained

options.label: D
options.text: Pulling back increases parasite drag from the larger frontal area of the pitched-up aircraft, which has a greater effect than the induced drag change and causes the aircraft to slow toward stall

questions.explanation: In powerless flight, the glide ratio is determined entirely by the L/D ratio. Best glide speed (Vg) occurs at L/D max — the airspeed where total drag is minimized. Flying SLOWER than Vg by pulling back increases the angle of attack, which causes induced drag to spike (induced drag increases with the inverse square of airspeed). The total drag increase steepens the descent angle, meaning the aircraft covers LESS ground distance for each foot of altitude lost. The pilot is achieving the opposite of their intention: the glide path steepens and the aircraft lands even shorter. The correct action for a short glide is to ADD POWER (if available) or accept the undershoot and choose an alternate, closer landing site. FAA-H-8083-3C Chapter 18 describes the 'stretching the glide' fallacy as a leading cause of stall/crash accidents during engine-failure scenarios.

questions.text: After an engine failure at 400 feet AGL on takeoff from a 5,000-foot runway, a pilot's instinct is to turn back and land on the departure runway. Assuming a standard training aircraft, why is this 'impossible turn' likely to be fatal at this altitude?

options.label: A
options.text: At 400 feet AGL, the aircraft is still in the departure corridor and ATC will not clear a return to the runway, creating a legal conflict that delays the pilot's response time

options.label: B
options.text: At 400 feet, the aircraft's indicated airspeed is still at Vy (best rate of climb), which is too fast to configure for a landing — the pilot would overshoot the runway on the return

options.label: C
options.text: The engine failure at 400 feet eliminates the aircraft's electrical system, which means the flaps cannot be extended for the return approach, forcing the pilot to attempt a no-flap landing at a speed too high for the available runway length

options.label: D
options.text: The 210+ degrees of turn required to realign with the runway demands bank angles that increase stall speed and descent rate — at 400 feet, the cumulative altitude loss during the turn and subsequent pull-out exceeds the altitude available, guaranteeing impact before reaching the runway

questions.explanation: The 'impossible turn' requires approximately 210° of heading change to realign with the runway (180° reversal + ~30° for offset and alignment). This turn requires bank, which increases the load factor and therefore stall speed. At typical pattern speeds near Vg, significant bank reduces the stall margin to near zero. Simultaneously, the banked, powerless aircraft descends at an accelerated rate — each degree of bank increases the vertical descent rate. At 400 feet AGL, the altitude budget is insufficient to accommodate the total altitude loss from: the turn itself (~300-500 feet), the rollout and alignment (~100-200 feet), and the landing flare (~50 feet). Typical safe turnback altitudes range from 800-1,200 feet AGL depending on aircraft performance. AC 61-67C identifies the low-altitude turnback as one of the most common fatal GA maneuvers. The pre-takeoff briefing ('below X feet, land straight ahead within 30° of the nose') pre-loads the correct decision.

questions.text: After an engine failure at 4,000 feet AGL, you have trimmed for Vg and identified a suitable field. You arrive at the High Key position (over the field at approximately 1,500 feet AGL) and realize you have significant excess altitude. What is the correct technique to shed the excess energy?

options.label: A
options.text: Fly S-turns or a forward slip to dissipate excess altitude while keeping the field within gliding distance, deploying flaps incrementally only when the field is assured

options.label: B
options.text: Deploy full flaps immediately to steepen the descent — the sooner you configure for landing, the more stabilized your approach will be when you reach the field

options.label: C
options.text: Extend the landing gear early (if retractable) and deploy full flaps simultaneously — maximizing drag from multiple sources is the fastest way to descend to a normal approach profile

options.label: D
options.text: Push the nose down to increase airspeed well above Vg — the higher speed will increase drag and dissipate the excess energy faster than any other technique

questions.explanation: In a powerless emergency, excess altitude is a GOOD problem — it's always better to be too high than too low. The correct technique to shed excess altitude is S-turns (alternating heading changes that increase the ground path without moving away from the field) or a forward slip (crossed controls that increase drag and descent rate without increasing airspeed). Flaps should be deployed INCREMENTALLY and ONLY when the field is absolutely assured. Premature flap deployment is an irreversible energy expenditure — if the pilot deploys full flaps and then realizes the field is farther than expected, retracting flaps causes a sudden lift loss that can result in landing short. The 'full flaps immediately' answer deploys flaps too early. The 'increase airspeed well above best glide' answer increases airspeed unnecessarily, trading the manageable excess altitude for excess kinetic energy that must then be dissipated during the approach. FAA-H-8083-3C Chapter 18 describes energy management for emergency landings.

questions.text: Your engine fails at 5,000 feet AGL over flat farmland. You pitch for Vg, trim, and begin the memory items. When you move the fuel selector from LEFT tank to BOTH, the engine restarts. What should your next action be?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue to the nearest airport immediately — the engine restarted, but fuel starvation from an incorrect selector position means the root cause is identified; land and inspect the fuel system before continuing the original flight

options.label: B
options.text: Shut the engine down again by returning the selector to LEFT — you need to verify that the LEFT tank is actually empty before trusting the engine, as the restart might be temporary fuel surge from the interconnect line

options.label: C
options.text: Declare an emergency on 121.5 MHz and request priority handling to the nearest airport — any engine failure, even one that restarts, requires an emergency declaration and a mandatory maintenance inspection before the next flight

options.label: D
options.text: Continue the original flight plan — the fuel selector was simply on the wrong tank, which is a common pilot error; now that it's on BOTH, the engine will operate normally for the remainder of the flight

questions.explanation: The engine restarted because fuel starvation from the incorrect selector position was the cause — switching to BOTH restored fuel flow. While the root cause appears identified (pilot error — wrong tank position), the correct action is to land at the nearest suitable airport. The fuel system may have additional issues: air may have entered the fuel lines during starvation, the tank that was selected may have a blocked vent or pickup, or the fuel quantity in that tank may have been misread. Landing promptly allows inspection and verification before continuing. The 'continue the flight plan' answer assumes the problem is fully resolved without verification — fuel starvation can recur if the underlying cause (blocked vent, pickup, or actual fuel quantity) hasn't been confirmed. The 'declare an emergency' answer overstates the response — while diverting is prudent, an emergency declaration isn't necessarily required for a resolved fuel selector issue.

questions.text: Your engine fails at 1,800 feet AGL during departure. Directly ahead is a large, flat, recently harvested soybean field. Behind you, 180 degrees, is the departure runway — 6,000 feet of paved surface with rescue equipment. You have practiced the impossible turn but never tested your turnback altitude in this specific aircraft. All four actions below are possible. Which is the SAFEST aeronautical decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Land in the soybean field without any attempt to reach the runway — any turn at all after an engine failure is too dangerous, and you should always land straight ahead no matter how much altitude you have

options.label: B
options.text: Pitch for Vg, assess your position and the wind, and if 1,800 feet exceeds your pre-briefed turnback altitude with adequate margin, execute the turn — if not, commit to the soybean field with a proper emergency approach to the upwind end

options.label: C
options.text: Turn back immediately without hesitation — you practiced this turn during training and know the aircraft can make it; the soybean field is an unprepared surface that could flip the aircraft on rollout

options.label: D
options.text: Turn back to the runway — 1,800 feet AGL is plenty of altitude, and the paved runway with rescue equipment is always safer than a dirt field with no emergency services

questions.sjt_rationale: The 'turn back for the runway' choice favors the runway based on its surface quality without analyzing the turnback geometry (get-there-itis) — 1,800 feet may or may not be sufficient depending on wind, density altitude, and aircraft weight. The 'practiced it, turn back' choice executes the turn based on past practice without considering current conditions (macho) — training conditions and the current scenario may differ significantly in wind, weight, and density altitude. The 'never turn, land straight ahead' choice refuses any turn regardless of altitude (resignation) — at sufficiently high altitudes, a turnback can be executed safely, and a rigid 'never turn' rule wastes a viable option. Stabilizing at best glide and then assessing is the active professional middle path: stabilize first (pitch for Vg), then apply the pre-briefed decision altitude that was set BEFORE the emergency, incorporating objective criteria rather than real-time emotional decision-making.
questions.explanation: The turnback decision must be made against a pre-briefed altitude, not in real-time under stress. The pre-takeoff briefing ('below X feet, straight ahead; above X feet, turnback may be possible') pre-loads the decision so the stressed brain executes a script rather than performing complex calculations. Typical turnback altitudes range from 800-1,200 feet AGL depending on aircraft type, weight, and wind. At 1,800 feet, a turnback may be viable — but only if the pilot has practiced it and established a personal minimum. FAA-H-8083-3C Chapter 18 describes the decision framework for engine failure after takeoff. AC 61-67C emphasizes that the turnback decision should never be made for the first time during an actual emergency.

questions.text: You are gliding toward a suitable field after an engine failure at 3,000 feet AGL. Your best glide speed is 65 knots. There is a strong 25-knot headwind. You calculate you will land approximately 200 feet short of the field if you maintain 65 knots. A second field, smaller but closer, is reachable at normal Vg. All four actions below are possible. Which is the SAFEST aeronautical decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Pull back to fly 5 knots slower than Vg — this will flatten the glide angle and stretch the distance to reach the better field

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately turn 90 degrees to find a third field with no headwind component — searching for a better option is always preferable to committing to an imperfect one

options.label: C
options.text: Increase speed 5-10 knots above Vg to improve ground coverage in the headwind, and target the closer field — the speed increase reduces time in the headwind, and the smaller but reachable field is safer than the better field that can't be reached

options.label: D
options.text: Maintain 65 knots and commit to reaching the first field — you have made tight approaches before, and 200 feet short means you will probably roll out into the field anyway

questions.sjt_rationale: The 'fly slower than best glide' choice flies slower than Vg (get-there-itis) — this is the 'stretching the glide' fallacy. Below Vg, induced drag spikes, the glide ratio worsens, and the aircraft lands even shorter. The 'commit to the first field' choice accepts landing 200 feet short of the field (macho) — 200 feet short means hitting whatever obstacle (fence, ditch, road) is at the boundary, not 'rolling into' the field. The 'search for a third field' choice abandons both identified fields to search for a third option (resignation) — at 3,000 feet in an emergency, committing to a known option beats searching. Adding speed above best glide for the headwind applies the correct headwind correction: flying 5-10 knots faster than Vg increases groundspeed, reducing the time spent fighting the headwind and increasing ground distance covered. It also correctly commits to the reachable field rather than the unreachable one.
questions.explanation: Wind correction for glide performance is a critical concept in powerless flight. Into a headwind, the aircraft should fly FASTER than Vg to increase groundspeed and reduce exposure time to the headwind. This trades altitude (descending slightly faster) for ground distance — the net effect is increased ground range into the wind. Conversely, with a tailwind, fly slightly slower than Vg. The 'stretching the glide' fallacy — pulling back to fly slower than Vg — always worsens the glide ratio because induced drag increases faster than the airspeed decrease saves parasite drag. FAA-H-8083-25C Chapter 5 describes the wind correction to Vg and its aerodynamic basis.
